contributions.headingText: Giant cell tumour of soft tissue is an intermediate, rarely metastasizing, multinodular, giant cell–rich neoplasm lacking keratin expression.
9251/1 Giant cell tumour of soft parts
2F7C & XH81M1 Neoplasms of uncertain behaviour of connective or other soft tissue & Giant cell tumour of soft parts NOS
Not recommended: giant cell tumour of low malignant potential.

Giant cell tumour of soft tissue usually occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the upper and lower extremities (70% of tumours). Affected less frequently are the trunk (20%) and head and neck (7%) regions {10496598; 10716152; 10680893; 19615796; 21563092}. Occasional cases have been reported in other anatomical locations {21139924; 23644334; 29867073}.
The tumours usually present as painless growing masses {10716152; 10680893}, with an average duration of 6 months {10680893}. Peripheral mineralization is common.

Giant cell tumour of soft tissue is rare and occurs predominantly in the fifth decade of life, but it can affect patients ranging in age from 5 to 89 years. Giant cell tumour of soft tissue shows no apparent difference in incidence with regard to sex or ethnicity {10496598; 10716152; 10680893}.

Giant cell tumour of soft tissue lacks H3-3A variants that are present in most giant cell tumours of bone, as well as HMGA2::NCOR2 fusions seen in keratin-positive giant cell–rich tumours, suggesting a distinct pathogenesis for each of the three entities, despite their morphological overlap {28084336; 28477388; 33742141}.

Tumours range in size from 7 to 100 mm (mean: 30 mm) {10496598; 10716152; 10680893}. Subcutaneous adipose tissue or dermis is involved in 70% of tumours; 30% are situated deep to superficial fascia. Giant cell tumour of soft tissue is a well-circumscribed, mostly solid, nodular mass with a fleshy, reddish-brown or grey cut surface. Gritty regions of mineralized bone are frequently present at the periphery {10716152}.

Giant cell tumour of soft tissue displays a characteristic multinodular architecture (85%) that is far more pronounced than that seen in giant cell tumour of bone. Cellular nodules are separated by fibrous septa of varying thickness, containing haemosiderin-laden macrophages {10716152}. The nodules are composed of a mixture of round to oval mononuclear cells and osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells, with both cell types immersed in a richly vascularized stroma. Mitotic activity is readily seen in giant cell tumour of soft tissue {10496598; 10716152; 10680893}. Nuclear pleomorphism and bizarre giant cells are absent, and necrosis is rarely found {10496598; 10716152; 10680893}. Metaplastic bone formation is present in approximately 50% of tumours, most often in the form of a peripheral shell of woven bone. Aneurysmal bone cyst–like changes may be seen. Vascular invasion is identified in about 30% of tumours {10496598; 10680893}. Additional histological features include stromal haemorrhage (50%) and regressive changes in the form of marked stromal fibrosis and clusters of foamy macrophages (70%). Giant cell tumour of soft tissue lacks keratin expression and peripheral lymphoid aggregates characteristic of keratin-positive giant cell–rich tumour {33742141}.

Cytology aspirates show variable cellularity, mononuclear polygonal cells, spindle cells in small tissue fragments, and plentiful large osteoclast-like giant cells (each with 10 or more nuclei) seen singly or in the tissue fragments, overall resembling the cytological features of giant cell tumour of bone {34618411}.
Essential: multinodular superficial soft tissue neoplasm; histiocytoid mononuclear cell population with osteoclastic giant cells; metaplastic bone formation is common; lack of keratin expression.
Giant cell tumour of soft tissue is associated with a local recurrence rate of 12%, with very rare metastasis {10496598; 10716152; 10680893}.
